_changelog: v1.0.0 (2026-10-16) first version, from latent-season9-bible-v1.0.0.md row a9e03 and writer brief a9e03-v1.0.0.md. a9e02's next field was honoured: forward-deployed discovery, the questions to ask, scoping the work and agreeing what success means. Keeps apart from a6e06: here the measure itself was never agreed; nothing went silent. Calls appear only as counts in the office's phone log. Timeline: discovery, one 45-minute meeting, Tuesday 8 September 2026; she chose 'resolved' (a chat that ends without 'talk to a person'), target 80%, alone; live Thursday 1 October; every chat starts by asking for the policy number; a chat ends when the client presses 'talk to a person', closes the window, or after 10 minutes idle. October: 600 chats, 54 asked for a person, 546 'resolved' (91%), green all month. Sunday 1 November: draft review emailed 21:40; at 22:10 the owner forwards the October phone log ('Then why are clients still ringing us twice?'); matched by policy number and topic within 48 hours, 210 of the 546 rang back; 546 - 210 = 336 of 600 done without a second contact (56%). The office is shut on Sundays, so chats on Friday 30 October lose no calls; the 17 chats of Saturday 31 October are counted with calls so far and rechecked on Tuesday 3 November. Given data, all in the sim: 48 thumbs-up (6 rang back); the 'anything else?' prompt moves 24 of the 54 to giving up and ringing (570 resolved, 234 rang, 336 done); September baseline from the September phone log, set once: 290 of 500 first calls (58%). Warn reply: paused Tuesday 3 to Monday 16 November, 14 days, 10 working days; about 271 questions back on the phones (600 x 14 / 31). Cold case: 3 months later, Monday 1 February 2027. Sources read 16 October 2026; The Mom Test is named only, since no readable text of its rules was found; the ISO 9001 and ISO/IEC 27001 pages are third-party listings; the PDPC page is named, not quoted.
title: The Client Who Doesn't Know

post.author: u/second_call_hallveig
post.title: I built a chat assistant for an insurance broker. Her October dashboard says 546 of 600 chats resolved. Her phone log says 210 of those clients rang the office anyway.

blocks.text: I work for a small consultancy. It sends me inside a client's business to build and launch its AI (artificial intelligence) system. The job is called forward-deployed engineer. My client is an independent insurance broker on the high street: 4 staff, about 1,800 clients, with home, landlord and small-shop cover.

She wanted an assistant on her website: a chat window where a language model, a program that writes text, answers questions about what a policy's wording says. It never says whether a claim will be paid. Each chat starts by asking for the policy number, so it opens the right wording.

My job starts with meetings where I learn how the client's work runs, before I build. That's called discovery. Ours was one 45-minute meeting, on Tuesday 8 September. First I asked which documents she had. Then which computer systems the office used. Last, who would pick up chats the assistant couldn't finish. My notes hold one line in the owner's words: 'I want clients to stop ringing us twice about the same thing.'
Afterwards, alone, I chose how we'd judge it. A number that says how well something works is a measure. The measure a project is judged by is its success metric.

A chat ends one of three ways. The client presses 'talk to a person', and the office replies by email. Or the client closes the window. Or 10 minutes pass with no message, and it closes itself. I counted the last two ways as success, and called them 'resolved'. Target: 80%.

It went on a screen of live numbers that turns green at or above the target: a dashboard. The owner saw a green screen, never a choice. We went live on Thursday 1 October. Each line below shows the month, measure, count and colour.

october  resolved          546 of 600 chats  91%  target 80%  green
october  talk to a person   54 of 600 chats
On Sunday 1 November I was building the first monthly review, for 09:00 on Monday. At 21:40 I emailed the owner the draft. At 22:10 she replied with the office's October phone log attached.

blocks.title: Re: October review (draft)
items: Then why are clients still ringing us twice?
blocks.sig: 22:10, Sunday 1 November. Attached: October phone log.

blocks.text: Staff type every call into that log: time, policy number, topic. The assistant files each chat under a topic from the same office list. I had never put the log beside the dashboard. I matched them in three steps. Take each resolved chat's policy number and end time. Find calls from that policy number within the next 48 hours. Keep those on the same topic.

The log ends on Saturday 31 October, and the office is shut on Sundays, so a chat on Friday 30 October loses no calls. For the 17 chats on the 31st, Monday is still to come: I counted calls so far, and I'll recheck on Tuesday. Each line below is a count from the match.

resolved chats                      546
rang within 48 hours, same topic    210
done without a second contact       546 - 210 = 336 of 600  56%
Every client who gave up and picked up the phone had counted as a win.

Top row: discovery on Tuesday 8 September, one 45-minute meeting with no question about success; the measure I chose alone, resolved, target 80%, which the owner never saw as a choice; launch on Thursday 1 October, every chat starting with the policy number; the October dashboard, 546 of 600, 91%, green all month. Bottom row: 54 of 600 chats pressed talk to a person and the office replied; 546 ended by closing the window or 10 minutes idle and counted as resolved; the phone log forwarded at 22:10 shows 210 of them rang within 48 hours about the same topic; done without a second contact, 546 minus 210, 336 of 600, 56%.

blocks.text: My dashboard was a scoreboard that counts walk-outs as wins. The review is at 09:00, ten hours away. In my notebook: what does success mean to you, and how will we both know? What should I change before Monday?

comments.author: u/gradient_ghost
comments.text: Nothing at that broker's is haunted. Your assistant did what you told the dashboard to count. One idea for Monday: the same number, taken before a change, tells you whether anything moved. That's called a baseline. And one for later: forward-deployed interviews have a discovery round, an interview stage where you question a pretend new client, and it tests exactly this night. Two questions. Before 1 October, how many clients rang twice about the same thing, and where would that be written down? And what has the owner ever agreed to, in writing?

replies.author: u/second_call_hallveig
replies.text: Before 1 October: the September phone log, the same sheet with time, policy number and topic. I haven't counted it. In writing, she has agreed to nothing. She has seen a green screen.

comments.author: u/green_means_go_eilert
comments.text: 546 of 600 is 91%, and 91% beats the 80% target. Clients ring twice whatever you build; some people just want a voice. Don't walk into Monday apologising for a green dashboard. If you want it higher, have the assistant ask 'anything else?' when a client goes quiet, before the chat can close, so fewer clients close the chat early. An 'anything else?' prompt, one line of instructions.

replies.author: u/green_means_go_eilert
replies.text: Owners always say that. Show her the green.

comments.author: u/let_them_vote_annegret
comments.text: Don't guess what resolved means; let the client say it. Each answer already has a button under it, a tap that means 'this helped': the thumbs-up. Count a chat as resolved only when the client presses it.

replies.author: u/second_call_hallveig
replies.text: 48 of the 600 chats got a thumbs-up in October.

comments.author: u/bigger_brain_siebren
comments.text: If 210 rang back, the answers weren't good enough. Switch to a bigger language model; it reads policy wording better, and it's one setting.

replies.author: u/second_call_hallveig
replies.text: The log says they rang. It doesn't say the answers were wrong; I haven't read one of the 210 yet. And it only answers what the wording says, never whether a claim will be paid. Where a rule on giving insurance advice applies, that line matters. Not legal advice.

reply.prompt: The review is at 09:00 on Monday 2 November, and the owner wants to know why clients still ring twice. What should I change? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Add 'anything else?' prompts so fewer clients close the chat early.
options.verdict: A greener number, the same calls
options.part2: On Monday I showed the owner the green dashboard and added the prompt that afternoon. When a client goes quiet, the assistant now asks 'anything else?' before the chat can close. November brought 600 chats again, much like October's. 24 clients who would have pressed 'talk to a person' answered the prompt instead, went round once more and left; all 24 rang the office within 48 hours. The dashboard read resolved: 570 of 600 (95%), greener than ever. The phone log said 234 rang back about the same topic: the 210, plus those 24. Done without a second contact: 570 - 234 = 336 of 600, exactly October's. At the next monthly review the owner forwarded the phone log again, with the same question.
options.senior: A prompt that keeps clients in the chat changes how chats end, not whether the question was answered. Here it moved 24 clients from 'asked for a person' to 'gave up and rang', and the measure counts giving up as success. When a number rises because leaving got harder, it is measuring the exit, not the outcome. Fix what the number means before you tune anything against it.

options.text: Count a chat as resolved only when the client presses thumbs-up.
options.verdict: Honest taps, too few to count
options.part2: On Monday I changed the rule: a chat counts as resolved only when the client presses thumbs-up. November brought 600 chats again, much like October's, and 48 got a thumbs-up. The dashboard read resolved: 48 of 600 (8%), red against the 80% target. The owner asked whether the assistant had broken. It hadn't. In the phone log, done without a second contact was still 336 of 600, and 6 of the 48 thumbs-up clients rang back anyway. The number swung from 91% to 8%, and the ringing never moved.
options.senior: A thumbs-up is the client's own signal, which beats a guess, but few people press it and those who do are not typical. 48 of 600 can't speak for the other 552, and 6 of the 48 still rang. Keep a button like this as one signal beside an agreed measure, never as the measure: it counts who taps, not whose problem went away.

options.text: Pause the assistant for two weeks of discovery with the office staff.
options.verdict: The right questions, at a price
options.part2: On Monday I proposed pausing the assistant from Tuesday 3 November for two weeks while I sat with the 4 staff, watched how they handle calls, and went through 100 recent phone-log lines with them. The owner agreed. October's 600 chats over 31 days is about 19 a day, so in the 14 days about 271 questions went back to the phones. The consultancy billed 10 working days of my time. The discovery itself was good: by Monday 16 November the owner had written her measure in her own words, and we had the September baseline from the phone log, 290 of 500. Under her measure, October read 336 of 600: a number I could have shown her on 2 November. She said she'd rather have asked the questions with the assistant still running.
options.senior: Stopping to do discovery properly asks the right questions: who contacts you and why, what success means to the client, what the number was before. But they didn't need the assistant switched off. The records that answer them, the phone logs, already existed, and an hour with the owner could agree the measure. Pause when a system is doing harm; this one was mis-measured, not dangerous, and the client paid for the fortnight twice, in fees and in phone calls.

options.text: Agree one measure in the owner's words, with a September baseline.
options.part2: At 09:00 on Monday 2 November I put two numbers in front of the owner. 'Resolved', the way I had counted it: 546 of 600. Done without a second contact about the same topic within 48 hours: 336 of 600. Then I asked what I should have asked on 8 September: what does success look like to you, and how will we both know? She wrote it on the review in her own words: a client who doesn't contact us again about the same question within 48 hours. We took the baseline from the September phone log, counted the same way and set once: of 500 first calls about a question, 290 had no second call on the same topic within 48 hours. The dashboard now counts 'resolved' her way: 336 of 600 (56%) beside September's 290 of 500 (58%), amber, a little below. The 17 chats from 31 October get rechecked on Tuesday, once their 48 hours are up. Then she asked the next question herself: what are the 210 ringing about? We booked Wednesday to read them together.
options.senior: A forward-deployed engineer's first job is to agree what success means, in the client's words, before building anything that reports it. Turn her sentence into a count she can check from her own records: no second contact about the same question within 48 hours, matched by policy number. Take the baseline from before launch, counted the same way, and fix it once. Then redefine the dashboard to match and show both numbers on the day, the flattering one and the true one. A green number nobody agreed is a guess; a smaller number she agreed is a measure.

sim.title: Re-count the broker's October
sim.lede: You're the forward-deployed engineer at 21:40 on Sunday 1 November 2026, the draft review just emailed, before the owner forwards the October phone log. No real model runs here: every count is given data. October, live from Thursday 1 October: 600 chats, each started with a policy number; 54 pressed 'talk to a person'; the other 546 ended when the client closed the window or after 10 minutes idle. Matched by policy number and topic, 210 of those 546 rang the office within 48 hours. The office is shut on Sundays, so chats on Friday 30 October lose no calls; the 17 chats of Saturday 31 October are counted with calls so far. 48 chats got a thumbs-up, and 6 of those rang back. With the 'anything else?' prompt, 24 of the 54 answer it instead of pressing 'talk to a person', then leave, and all 24 ring. September, before the assistant, from the September phone log, counted the same way and set once (late-September calls checked against early October's log): 290 of 500 first calls had no second call on the same topic within 48 hours. Each reply is played on a month like October: the same 600 chats. Colour: green at or above the 80% target, red below; the agreed measure has no target yet and shows amber below the September baseline.
sim.tryThis: Try this: press match to bring in the 22:10 phone log. 210 rang back, and done without a second contact is 336 of 600, while the dashboard still says 546, green. Turn the 'anything else?' prompt on: resolved climbs to 570 of 600, and done stays 336. Switch success to thumbs-up only: 48 of 600, red. Switch to the agreed measure, then look at September's baseline. Then play each reply.

explain.oneLine: Nothing at the broker's was haunted. 'Resolved' counted every chat that didn't ask for a person, so a client who gave up and rang the office counted as a win: 600 - 54 = 546, green, while the phone log showed 210 of them rang within 48 hours about the same topic, leaving 336 of 600 done. The engineer chose the measure alone; the owner's own words, 'stop ringing us twice', were never turned into a number she agreed.

steps.title: How a walk-out became a win.
steps.text: A chat ends in one of three ways. First, the client presses 'talk to a person', and the office replies by email: 54 of 600. Second, the client closes the window. Third, 10 minutes pass with no message, and the chat closes itself. 'Resolved' counted every chat that ended the second or third way: 600 - 54 = 546, 91%, above the 80% target, so the dashboard was green. What can go wrong: a client who gives up and closes the window looks exactly like a client who got the answer. The count can't tell them apart, so it scored both as wins, like a scoreboard that counts walk-outs. Unlike a6e06 (watching a system in production), nothing here broke or went silent: the system worked as built, and the measure itself was never agreed.

steps.title: Putting the chats beside the phone log.
steps.text: Every chat starts with the client's policy number, and staff type the time, policy number and topic of every call. The match runs in three steps. First, take each resolved chat's policy number and the time it ended. Second, find calls from that policy number within the next 48 hours. Third, keep only calls on the same topic as the chat. 210 of the 546 matched, so 546 - 210 = 336 of 600 were done without a second contact, 56%. The log ends on Saturday 31 October and the office is shut on Sundays, so only the 17 chats of 31 October still had hours to run; their calls so far are counted, and they get rechecked on Tuesday. What can go wrong: a policy number is personal data, so matching is a new use of it that needs care, and a client who rings about a different topic slips through.

steps.title: Discovery: the questions that come before the build.
steps.text: The meeting on 8 September asked about documents and systems. A fuller discovery asks, in order: who contacts you, and why (read 100 recent contacts, not a summary of them); what happens today, step by step, when a client asks; what success looks like, in your words; who decides whether it worked; what the number is today, the baseline; what must never happen (here, telling a client whether a claim will be paid); and what is out of scope (anything but policy wording). Write the answers down and send them back for the client to correct. What can go wrong: skip the success question, and the engineer answers it alone, which is what happened here.

steps.title: One agreed measure, a baseline, and both numbers on the day.
steps.text: The owner's words were already in the notes: stop ringing us twice about the same thing. As a count: chats with no second contact about the same topic within 48 hours. The baseline comes from the September phone log, counted the same way and set once. A first call is one with no call from that policy number on that topic in the 48 hours before it; of 500 first calls, 290 had no second call within 48 hours, 58%. October: 336 of 600, 56%. Redefine 'resolved' to match, and show the old and the new number at Monday's review. What can go wrong: an 'anything else?' prompt or a thumbs-up rule moves the old number (570 of 600, or 48 of 600) and leaves the new one at 336, so only the agreed measure says whether the problem moved.

diagram.aria: The fix. Top row: the owner's words, stop ringing us twice; the agreed measure, no second contact within 48 hours, written down; the September baseline, 290 of 500, set once from the phone log; the dashboard, 336 of 600, amber, with the old rule's 546 shown beside it. Bottom row: the chats, each starting with a policy number, and the phone log with time, policy number and topic, both feeding the match on same policy number and topic within 48 hours, which feeds the dashboard.

explain.caption: Read the top row left to right: the owner's sentence becomes one measure she wrote down, its September baseline is counted once from the phone log, and the dashboard shows the new count beside the old one. Bottom row: the chats and the phone log meet in the match, by policy number and topic within 48 hours, and the match feeds the dashboard.

fix.title: The fix: one measure in her words, a baseline, and both numbers
fix.text: Go back to the owner before the review and turn her own sentence into a count she agrees in writing: chats with no second contact about the same topic within 48 hours, matched by policy number against the office's phone log. Take the September baseline from the September phone log, counted the same way, and set it once: 290 of 500. Redefine 'resolved' on the dashboard to match. On Monday show both numbers, 546 of 600 under the old rule and 336 of 600 under hers, and say what the gap is: clients who gave up and rang. Then ask the discovery questions skipped in September, starting with what the 210 were ringing about.

limits: September counts first calls and October counts chats: the same question in the owner's words, asked of two kinds of first contact. Close enough to compare, not identical, and the review should say so.

The match sees only the same policy number and the same topic. A client who rings from a partner's policy, or about a different topic that grew from the chat, slips through, so 210 is a floor, not an exact count.
Matching chats to call records is a new use of clients' personal data. Where data protection rules apply, the clients may need telling and the match should be kept to this purpose.

explain.seniorTake: A forward-deployed engineer's first deliverable isn't the system; it's the definition of success the client agrees to. Ask who contacts them and why, what happens today, what success looks like in their words, who decides, what the number is today, what must never happen and what is out of scope, and write the answers down. Turn the success answer into a count from the client's own records, take the baseline before launch, counted the same way, and fix it. A measure you pick alone can go green while the client's problem stays. The discovery and customer rounds of a forward-deployed interview loop test this skill: expect 'you join a new client: what are your first questions, and what is your baseline?'

realWorld.title: Google PAIR: agree what success and failure look like
realWorld.text: The People + AI Guidebook chapter User Needs + Defining Success says: Everyone on your team should feel aligned on what both success and failure look like for your feature, and how to alert the team if something goes wrong. For a forward-deployed engineer the team includes the client; here only the engineer knew what 'resolved' meant.

realWorld.title: Google PAIR: the pull towards a narrow measure
realWorld.text: The same chapter warns: Like any definition of success, it will be tempting to make it very simple, narrow, and immediate. 'Ended without asking for a person' is all three.

realWorld.title: Rules of Machine Learning, Rule #2: metrics first
realWorld.text: Martin Zinkevich's Rule #2 is First, design and implement metrics, and it opens: Before formalizing what your machine learning system will do, track as much as possible in your current system. The broker's phone log was that record: a September baseline existed before launch, uncounted.

realWorld.title: Rules of Machine Learning, Rule #13: a proxy for the true objective
realWorld.text: Rule #13 says: The ML objective should be something that is easy to measure and is a proxy for the "true" objective. It also notes: Further, different team members often can't agree on the true objective. 'Resolved' was an easy proxy; the true objective was in the owner's sentence, and she was never asked to agree.

realWorld.title: The Mom Test: a book on asking customers
realWorld.text: Rob Fitzpatrick's The Mom Test is subtitled How to talk to customers & learn if your business is a good idea when everyone is lying to you. It is named here as further reading on asking clients useful questions; its rules are not quoted, since no readable text of them was checked.

realWorld.title: ISO 9001:2015: requirements, then measurement
realWorld.text: A third-party listing of the standard's clauses gives 8.2 Requirements for products and services and 9.1 Monitoring, measurement, analysis and evaluation. Agreeing what success means with the client sits under the first; counting it from records sits under the second.

realWorld.title: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 A.5.34: privacy and protection of PII
realWorld.text: A third-party guide titles the control Privacy and Protection of PII and says it covers the storage, privacy and protection of Personal Identifiable Information (PII) in all its forms. Matching chats to calls by policy number is such a use; check the wording in your own copy of the standard.

asked: You join a new client: what are your first questions, and what is your baseline?
Your dashboard is green, but the client says nothing has changed. What do you do?
interview.answer: Before building, I run discovery. First, who contacts you and why: I read 100 recent contacts myself, not a summary. Then what happens today, step by step, when a client asks. Then what success looks like in the client's own words, and who decides whether we got there. Then the number today, the baseline, counted from their own records the same way I'll count it after launch, and fixed once. Then what must never happen and what is out of scope. I write it all down and the client corrects it, so the success metric is agreed in writing before anything reports it. If a dashboard is green while the client says nothing changed, I assume the measure is wrong before the client is: I put my number beside their own records, find where they disagree, and go back to their words. At an insurance broker that meant matching chats to the phone log by policy number: 546 of 600 'resolved', but only 336 of 600 done without a second contact, against a September baseline of 290 of 500.

The id on a client's policy. Every chat starts by asking for it, and staff type it into the phone log, which is how chats and calls are matched.
A request to the insurer to pay out under a policy. Whether a claim will be paid is out of scope for the assistant.
A firm hired by other businesses to do specialist work for them. The storyteller's sends engineers into clients' businesses.
An engineer who works inside a client's business to build and launch its AI system: asking the questions, building, measuring and handing over.
Short for artificial intelligence: here, software built on a language model that answers questions in plain text.
The broker's website chat window, where a language model answers questions about policy wording. Live from Thursday 1 October.
A program that reads text and writes text back, one likely piece at a time, like a phone's next-word suggestions grown huge (a1e03).
A larger model, usually slower and dearer, that tends to write better. One commenter's idea; the answers were never what was mis-measured.
The meetings where a forward-deployed engineer learns how the client's work runs, what success means to them and what is out of scope, before building.
An interview stage for forward-deployed roles where you question a pretend new client: what you ask first, and how you'll both know it worked.
A number that says how well something works, counted the same way each time, such as 546 of 600 chats resolved.

The level a measure should reach. 'Resolved' had 80%, and the dashboard turned green at or above it.

The chat button that hands a chat to the office, which replies by email. 54 of October's 600 chats ended this way.
With no message from the client. After 10 minutes idle a chat closes itself, and 'resolved' counted it as a success.
The office's record of every call, typed by staff: time, policy number and topic. Calls appear in this case only as counts from it.
The subject of a chat or call, from one office list. The match keeps only calls on the same topic as the chat.
A call from the same policy number about the same topic within 48 hours of a chat or first call: the client asking again.

An easy number standing in for the one you really care about. 'Resolved' was a proxy for clients not ringing twice, and a poor one.

atWork: Look for a success number nobody agreed with the client. It is a common pattern: an engineer picks something easy to count, such as chats that didn't ask for a person, puts a target on it, and the dashboard goes green while the client's own records say nothing changed. Ask four things. Who chose this measure, and has the client written down, in their own words, what success means? What did it read before launch, counted from the client's own records the same way? Can it count a client who gave up as a success? And who decides whether it worked? Then put your number beside a record the client trusts, such as their phone log, and read where the two disagree. Build Night: this case feeds no Build Night milestone; the season finale, a full forward-deployed engineer simulation, opens with this discovery. Standards-readiness note, as these apply to you and not legal advice: where an organisation works to ISO 9001:2015, clause 8.2 (requirements for products and services) is likely to expect requirements agreed and reviewed with the customer, and clause 9.1 (monitoring, measurement, analysis and evaluation) to expect a decision on what is measured and how; an agreed metric with a recorded baseline is evidence for both. Matching chats to call records by policy number is a new use of personal data: where ISO/IEC 27001:2022 applies, control A.5.34 (privacy and protection of PII) covers it, and for Singapore's DPTM, the PDPA's purpose limitation and consent obligations apply where chats are matched to call records. Tell clients, and match only for the stated purpose. Building this in now costs far less than rebuilding the measure, or the consent, at audit time.

recall.prompt: A colleague launched a returns assistant for a bike shop in March. Her dashboard shows 'handled: 470 of 500', counting every chat that didn't end with 'get me a human'. The shop manager says the returns desk is as busy as ever. What is wrong with her number, and what should she do next?

keyIdeas.idea: The number counts customers who gave up as successes, because a chat that ends without asking for a human isn't the same as a solved problem
Check against the shop's own records: match each chat to the desk's log and count customers who came back, a second contact
Agree one measure with the manager in his words, in writing, with a baseline from before launch

recall.model: Her number counts every chat that didn't ask for a human, so a customer who gave up and walked to the desk counts as a success. She should check the shop's own records: match each 'handled' chat to the desk's log and count customers who came back about the same return within a few days, a second contact. Then sit with the manager, agree the measure in his words, in writing, with a baseline from the desk's log before launch, and redefine 'handled' to match.

recall.prompt: October: 600 chats. 54 pressed 'talk to a person'. Of the other 546, 210 rang the office within 48 hours about the same topic. How many were done without a second contact?
recall.why: The 54 who asked for a person needed the office, and the 210 rang back, so neither is done. 600 - 54 = 546 'resolved'; 546 - 210 = 336 of 600, 56%.

recall.prompt: An interviewer says: you've just joined a new client as a forward-deployed engineer. Walk me through your first week, before you write any code.

keyIdeas.idea: Find out who contacts the client and why, from real recent contacts, and what happens today
Get success in the client's own words, written down, and who decides
Take a baseline from the client's own records before launch, counted the same way
Settle what must never happen and what is out of scope

recall.model: I'd run discovery first. Who contacts you and why: I'd read 100 recent contacts, not a summary. What happens today, step by step. What success looks like in their own words, written down, and who decides whether it worked. The number today, the baseline, counted from their own records the same way I'll count it after launch. What must never happen, and what is out of scope. I'd end the week with the success metric agreed in writing, before anything reports it.

recall.prompt: Which change raises 'resolved' while done without a second contact stays at 336 of 600?
options: An 'anything else?' prompt before the chat can close
Reading 100 recent calls with the owner
Matching chats to calls by policy number
Pausing the assistant for two weeks
recall.why: 24 of the 54 who would have pressed 'talk to a person' answer the prompt, give up and ring instead. 'Resolved' becomes 570 of 600 and rang back 234, so done is 570 - 234 = 336 of 600: the same.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 3 months later. The broker's dashboard now counts her measure every month. On Monday 1 February I started with a new client: a garden centre with a web shop, where an assistant will answer plant-care questions. At the first meeting the manager said: 'I want people to stop bringing dead plants back.' Before I arrived, a colleague had put a success metric in the plan: the share of chats where the customer clicks a product link, target 30%. The manager nodded at it.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. What should she do about the success metric before she builds anything?

keyIdeas.idea: A click is a proxy the builder picked; the manager's words are about plants coming back, and clicks can rise while that doesn't move
Agree one measure with the manager in his own words, in writing, and who decides
Take a baseline from the centre's own records before launch, counted the same way, set once

coldCase.model: A product-link click is a proxy someone picked; the manager asked for fewer dead plants coming back, and clicks can go green while plants returned don't move. Go back to him and agree one measure in his own words, in writing, and who decides whether it worked: for example, plants returned within 30 days of a plant-care chat. Then take a baseline from the centre's own records before launch, its returns log for last autumn, counted the same way and set once. Show both numbers from the first review.
